title: Quantum many-body effects in the optical response of ideal thin films
authors: David Trejo-Garcia, Tapio T. Rantala, Marco Ornigotti, Juha Tiihonen
abstract: We study quantum many-body effects in the long-wavelength optical response of confined electrons at finite temperatures. We simulate homogeneous electron gas confined in one dimension into a slab of nanoscale thickness. We demonstrate how the slab boundaries break down the ideal Drude response of free charge carriers, giving rise to scattering effects due to both the surfaces and quantum many-body interactions. We use a recent path-integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) approach developed in [Tiihonen et al. Phys. Rev. A 113, 053711] to quantify these effects in high accuracy. We perform phenomenological fits to Drude and Drude-Lorentz models parameters, manifesting various trends of the optical response with physical parameters like density and temperature, and numerical effects like finite size and the quantum statistics.
summary: This paper uses Path-integral Monte Carlo simulations to study how confining electrons in thin slabs affects their optical response. It demonstrates that the boundaries break the ideal Drude behavior, leading to measurable scattering effects quantified by fitting the response to Drude and Drude-Lorentz models. The findings are important for understanding charge transport in nanoscale quantum materials.
main_problem: The study investigates quantum many-body effects on the long-wavelength optical response of confined electrons at finite temperatures.
main_result: Slab confinement significantly breaks down the ideal Drude response, causing measurable scattering effects, particularly in the out-of-plane optical susceptibility.
method: The authors employ the Path-integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) method to simulate the system's dynamics and analyze the optical response via the imaginary-time dipole autocorrelation function.
model_or_system: The system modeled is an ideal homogeneous electron gas (HEG) confined within a quasi-2D slab geometry, allowing for the study of boundary effects on electron interactions.
key_observables: Optical susceptibility $\chi(\omega)$, the imaginary-time dipole autocorrelation function $	ilde{G}(	au)$, and fitted parameters for the Drude ($\Gamma_D$) and Drude-Lorentz ($\Gamma_{DL}, \omega_0$) models.
important_parameters: Slab thickness ($2R$), particle density ($r_s$), finite temperature ($\Theta$), and the ratio of confinement size to thermal wavelength ($2R/\Lambda$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting the PIMC data to Drude/Drude-Lorentz models for analytic continuation, and the PIMC method itself is limited by the Fermion sign problem.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of fitted parameters ($\Gamma_D, \Gamma_{DL}, \omega_0$) on slab thickness relative to thermal wavelength and density, and compare results between fermionic and classical (Boltzmannon) simulations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the breakdown of the ideal Drude response due to confinement. It details the PIMC methodology for calculating the optical response, presents quantitative results by fitting the imaginary-time correlation function to established models, and concludes by comparing the effects of quantum statistics and geometry.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, first-principles simulation of how geometric confinement and quantum statistics modify fundamental optical properties, which is crucial for designing nanoscale electronic devices.
